claim: Early-onset generalized torsion dystonia (DYT1) is an autosomal dominant movement disorder, commonly caused by a GAG base-pair deletion in the TOR1A gene coding for torsinA protein.
source: Early-onset generalized torsion dystonia (DYT1) is an autosomal dominant movement disorder, commonly caused by a GAG base-pair deletion in the TOR1A gene coding for torsinA protein, without gross brain structural defects or other detectable neuropathology (Ozelius et al., 1997; Ledoux et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ozelius et al., 1997; Ledoux et al., 2013).

claim: DYT1 dystonia occurs without gross brain structural defects or other detectable neuropathology.
source: Early-onset generalized torsion dystonia (DYT1) is an autosomal dominant movement disorder, commonly caused by a GAG base-pair deletion in the TOR1A gene coding for torsinA protein, without gross brain structural defects or other detectable neuropathology (Ozelius et al., 1997; Ledoux et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ozelius et al., 1997; Ledoux et al., 2013).

claim: Only 30–40% of DYT1 mutation carriers develop dystonia.
source: Intriguingly, only 30–40% of DYT1 mutation carriers develop dystonia, typically in childhood-early adolescence (Bressman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Bressman et al., 2000).

claim: DYT1 dystonia typically develops in childhood-early adolescence.
source: Intriguingly, only 30–40% of DYT1 mutation carriers develop dystonia, typically in childhood-early adolescence (Bressman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Bressman et al., 2000).

claim: Mutation carriers that do not develop symptoms during the critical developmental period remain unaffected for their entire life.
source: However, what triggers the clinical onset of symptoms is currently unknown, although the presence of a critical developmental period of susceptibility is highly probable, since mutation carriers that do not develop symptoms in that time-window remain unaffected for their entire life (Pappas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Pappas et al., 2014).

claim: A significantly enhanced responsiveness to plasticity protocols has been reported in dystonic patients.
source: A significantly enhanced responsiveness to plasticity protocols has been reported in dystonic patients (Edwards et al., 2006; Weise et al., 2006; Quartarone et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Edwards et al., 2006; Weise et al., 2006; Quartarone et al., 2009).

claim: Patterns of impaired motor learning have been described even in clinically unaffected DYT1 mutation carriers.
source: Moreover, patterns of impaired motor learning have been described even in clinically unaffected DYT1 mutation carriers (Ghilardi et al., 2003), further supporting the notion that aberrant plasticity represents a unique endophenotype in dystonia.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Ghilardi et al., 2003).

claim: An impairment of striatal plasticity has been demonstrated in a number of different DYT1 models, including transgenic mice and rats overexpressing mutant torsinA.
source: Of note, an impairment of striatal plasticity has been demonstrated in a number of different DYT1 models, including transgenic mice and rats overexpressing mutant torsinA (Martella et al., 2009; Grundmann et al., 2012), knock-in mice heterozygous for Δgag-torsinA (Dang et al., 2012; Martella et al., 2014; Rittiner et al., 2016), revealing an impressive similarity with studies of synaptic plasticity in human dystonia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Martella et al., 2009; Grundmann et al., 2012; Dang et al., 2012; Martella et al., 2014; Rittiner et al., 2016).

claim: An impairment of striatal plasticity has been demonstrated in knock-in mice heterozygous for Δgag-torsinA.
source: Of note, an impairment of striatal plasticity has been demonstrated in a number of different DYT1 models, including transgenic mice and rats overexpressing mutant torsinA (Martella et al., 2009; Grundmann et al., 2012), knock-in mice heterozygous for Δgag-torsinA (Dang et al., 2012; Martella et al., 2014; Rittiner et al., 2016), revealing an impressive similarity with studies of synaptic plasticity in human dystonia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Dang et al., 2012; Martella et al., 2014; Rittiner et al., 2016).

claim: SPNs recorded at P26 from both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag mice did not display firing activity at rest.
source: SPNs recorded at P26 from both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag mice did not display firing activity at rest and exhibited no significant differences in their intrinsic membrane properties (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: SPNs recorded at P26 from both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag mice exhibited no significant differences in their intrinsic membrane properties.
source: SPNs recorded at P26 from both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag mice did not display firing activity at rest and exhibited no significant differences in their intrinsic membrane properties (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Short ISI (25–50 ms) of paired synaptic stimulation induced PPF in both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag genotypes.
source: Short ISI (25–50 ms) of paired synaptic stimulation induced PPF in both genotypes (Figure 1B; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: At longer ISI (100–1000 ms), PPF was not observed in juvenile Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: At longer ISI (100–1000 ms), PPF was not observed in juvenile Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 1B; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: Glutamatergic sEPSCs did not differ between Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag genotypes at P26.
source: Glutamatergic sEPSCs did not differ between genotypes (Figure 1C; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: There was a significant increase in the amplitude, but not in the frequency, of mEPSCs recorded from Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to wild types at P26.
source: However, we found a significant increase in the amplitude, but not in the frequency, of mEPSCs recorded from Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to wild types (Figure 1D; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: GABAergic sIPSCs were unchanged in Tor1a+/Δgag with respect to Tor1a+/+ littermates at P26.
source: Conversely, GABAergic sIPSCs were unchanged in Tor1a+/Δgag with respect to Tor1a+/+ littermates (Figure 1E; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: mIPSCs were similar in both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag genotypes at P26.
source: Also, mIPSCs were similar in both genotypes (Figure 1F; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: In Tor1a+/+ SPNs, HFS failed to induce LTD from P15 to P27.
source: In Tor1a+/+ SPNs, HFS failed to induce LTD from P15 to P27 (Figure 2A; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: The HFS protocol elicited a robust LTD in Tor1a+/+ SPNs from P28 to P35.
source: Conversely, the HFS protocol elicited a robust LTD from P28 to P35 (Figure 2A; 59.63 ± 2.63% of control; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: In slices from Tor1a+/Δgag mice, HFS stimulation failed to cause a synaptic depression, independently from the postnatal day of recording.
source: Surprisingly, in slices from Tor1a+/Δgag mice, HFS stimulation failed to cause a synaptic depression, independently from the postnatal day of recording (Figure 2B; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: The LTP induction protocol failed to elicit a potentiation in Tor1a+/+ mice from P15 to P23.
source: The LTP induction protocol failed to elicit a potentiation in Tor1a+/+ mice from P15 to P23 (Partridge et al., 2000) (Figure 2C; p>0.05), whereas a stable LTP occurred from P24 to P35 (Figure 2C; 148.80 ± 15.39% of control; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance p>0.05 and a citation to prior research (Partridge et al., 2000).

claim: A stable LTP occurred in Tor1a+/+ mice from P24 to P35.
source: The LTP induction protocol failed to elicit a potentiation in Tor1a+/+ mice from P15 to P23 (Partridge et al., 2000) (Figure 2C; p>0.05), whereas a stable LTP occurred from P24 to P35 (Figure 2C; 148.80 ± 15.39% of control; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: In Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs LTP could be evoked as early as P15, revealing a premature onset.
source: Unexpectedly, in Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs LTP could be evoked as early as P15, revealing a premature onset, and showed a tendency to increase, compared to wild types (Figure 2D; Tor1a+/Δgag P15-23, 174.68 ± 22.59% of control; P24-35, 172.35 ± 11.06% of control; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: Neither ENK-positive nor ENK-negative SPNs exhibited LTD in Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Enkephalin staining revealed that neither ENK-positive nor ENK-negative SPNs exhibited LTD, ruling out a possible segregation to a specific population of SPNs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using immunohistochemistry.

claim: At P26, the NMDAR/AMPAR ratio was significantly reduced in Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs compared to wild types.
source: We found that, at P26, the NMDAR/AMPAR ratio was significantly reduced in Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs compared to wild types (Figure 3A; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: No significant differences in NMDAR/AMPAR ratio were recorded in P60 SPNs of both genotypes.
source: Conversely, no significant differences were recorded in P60 SPNs of both genotypes (Figure 3B; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs showed a significantly increased AMPAR current at hyperpolarized voltage ranges at P26.
source: Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs showed a significantly increased current at hyperpolarized voltage ranges (Figure 3C; 2-way ANOVA, p<0.01;HP= −70 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: No significant difference in RI was observed between Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag genotypes at P26.
source: We observed no significant difference in RI between genotypes (Figure 3C; p>0.05), suggesting that the enhanced AMPAR current involves an increased surface expression of AMPARs, rather than an altered receptor composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: The enhanced AMPAR current in Tor1a+/Δgag mice involves an increased surface expression of AMPARs, rather than an altered receptor composition.
source: We observed no significant difference in RI between genotypes (Figure 3C; p>0.05), suggesting that the enhanced AMPAR current involves an increased surface expression of AMPARs, rather than an altered receptor composition.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing no change in RI despite increased current.

claim: No significant difference in the RI of P26 SPNs was measured in the presence of NASPM.
source: No significant difference in the RI of P26 SPNs was measured in the presence of NASPM (Figure 3D; p>0.05); yet, at hyperpolarized voltage ranges AMPAR-mediated current was still increased in Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs (Figure 3D; two-way ANOVA, p<0.01 at HP =−70 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: At hyperpolarized voltage ranges AMPAR-mediated current was still increased in Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs in the presence of NASPM.
source: No significant difference in the RI of P26 SPNs was measured in the presence of NASPM (Figure 3D; p>0.05); yet, at hyperpolarized voltage ranges AMPAR-mediated current was still increased in Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs (Figure 3D; two-way ANOVA, p<0.01 at HP =−70 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: The normalized IV relationship of NMDAR-EPSCs showed no significant difference in the voltage-dependence of NMDARs between genotypes at P26.
source: The normalized IV relationship of NMDAR-EPSCs showed the characteristic 'J-shape' (Mayer et al., 1984) in SPNs recorded at P26 from both genotypes (Figure 3E). No significant difference was found in the voltage-dependence of NMDARs (p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance p>0.05 and a citation to prior research (Mayer et al., 1984).

claim: A significantly decreased decay time of NMDAR currents was detected in Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to controls at P26.
source: By analyzing the kinetics of the response at HP =+ 40 mV, we detected a significantly decreased decay time in Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to controls (Figure 3F,G; p<0.05), despite a comparable rise time, suggesting a modification of NMDAR subunit composition (Paoletti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G with statistical significance p<0.05 and a citation to prior research (Paoletti et al., 2013).

claim: There was a significant increase in the levels of both GluA1 and GluA2 AMPAR subunits in the postsynaptic compartment of P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to controls.
source: We found a significant increase in the levels of both GluA1 and GluA2 AMPAR subunits in the postsynaptic compartment of P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to controls (Figure 4A,B; p<0.05), consistent with the observed reduction of the NMDA/AMPA ratio and the absence of any alteration of the RI (see Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: There was an increase of phosphorylation at GluA1-Ser845 in P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Interestingly, we also found an increase of phosphorylation at GluA1-Ser845 (Figure 4A,B;, p<0.05), which is known to be correlated with LTP expression and to prevent endocytosis of GluA1-containing AMPARs (Oh et al., 2006; Bassani et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B with statistical significance p<0.05 and citations to prior research (Oh et al., 2006; Bassani et al., 2013).

claim: An increase of GluN2A but not GluN2B subunit was observed at postsynaptic sites of P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to Tor1a+/+.
source: Moreover, in agreement with the reduction of the NMDAR decay time, we observed an increase of GluN2A but not GluN2B subunit at postsynaptic sites of P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to Tor1a+/+ (Figure 4C,D; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: No modifications of PSD-95 was observed in P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Finally, no modifications of PSD-95, the most abundant scaffolding protein at the excitatory synapse, was observed (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Alterations of AMPAR and NMDAR subunits were not present in SPNs from P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Notably, these alterations of AMPAR and NMDAR subunits were not present in SPNs from P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 4; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: P26 Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs exhibited a higher number of mushroom-type spines compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
source: P26 Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs (Figure 5A–D) exhibited a higher number of mushroom-type spines (Figure 5C; p<0.05) and, consequently, a concomitant overall increase of dendritic spine width compared to Tor1a+/+ mice (Figure 5B; p<0.05), thus suggesting an advanced stage of spine maturation, in agreement with the observed molecular GluN2A/GluN2B switch (see Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: P26 Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs exhibited a concomitant overall increase of dendritic spine width compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
source: P26 Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs (Figure 5A–D) exhibited a higher number of mushroom-type spines (Figure 5C; p<0.05) and, consequently, a concomitant overall increase of dendritic spine width compared to Tor1a+/+ mice (Figure 5B; p<0.05), thus suggesting an advanced stage of spine maturation, in agreement with the observed molecular GluN2A/GluN2B switch (see Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: P26 Tor1a+/Δgag SPNs exhibited an overall decrease of dendritic spine density.
source: This event was associated, as expected, to an overall decrease of dendritic spine density (Figure 5A; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice showed a normalization of dendritic spine density compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
source: Conversely, P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 5E–H) showed a normalization of dendritic spine density (Figure 5E; p>0.05) and of spine width (Figure 5F; p>0.05) compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice showed a normalization of spine width compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
source: Conversely, P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 5E–H) showed a normalization of dendritic spine density (Figure 5E; p>0.05) and of spine width (Figure 5F; p>0.05) compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: At P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice showed an increase of thin spines compared to Tor1a+/+ mice.
source: Yet, at P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice showed an increase of thin spines compared to Tor1a+/+ mice (Figure 5G; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: BDNF expression profile showed a similar age-dependent time-course in both Tor1a+/+ and Tor1a+/Δgag genotypes.
source: BDNF expression profile showed a similar age-dependent time-course in both genotypes (Figure 6A,B; P15 vs P26: Tor1a+/+ p<0.05; Tor1a+/Δgagp<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B with statistical significance.

claim: Both proBDNF and BDNF levels were increased at P26 in Tor1a+/Δgag striatum.
source: Both proBDNF and BDNF levels were increased at P26 in Tor1a+/Δgag striatum (Figure 6C; proBDNF p<0.01, BDNF p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical significance.

claim: Quantitative PCR revealed an increased Bdnf expression in Tor1a+/Δgag cortex as compared to Tor1a+/+.
source: Quantitative PCR revealed an increased Bdnf expression in Tor1a+/Δgag cortex as compared to Tor1a+/+ (Figure 6D; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: No significant difference between genotypes was measured in the proBDNF and BDNF striatal protein levels in adult mice.
source: No significant difference between genotypes was measured in the proBDNF and BDNF striatal protein levels in adult mice (Figure 6E; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: Repetitive treatment with ANA-12 completely rescued corticostriatal LTD expression in P28-35 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: However, repetitive treatment with ANA-12 (0.5 mg/kg, intraperitoneal, 12 hr and 4 hr before the experiment; Cazorla et al., 2011; Stragier et al., 2015), completely rescued corticostriatal LTD expression in P28-35 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 7A; p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A with statistical significance p<0.05 and citations to prior research (Cazorla et al., 2011; Stragier et al., 2015).

claim: ANA-12 treatment reduced LTP amplitude in P24-35 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Additionally, ANA-12 treatment reduced LTP amplitude in P24-35 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 7B; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: In vivo treatment with ANA-12 totally normalized the IV curve of AMPAR-EPSC in P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Likewise, in vivo treatment with ANA-12 totally normalized the IV curve of AMPAR-EPSC in P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 7C; p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: In vivo treatment with ANA-12 failed to restore corticostriatal LTD in P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: Finally, to demonstrate that BDNF alterations occur in a defined time-window, we tested the effect of ANA-12 on corticostriatal LTD expression in adult Tor1a+/Δgag mice. In vivo treatment with ANA-12 (0.5 mg/kg, intraperitoneal, two administrations at 12 hr and 4 hr before the experiment) failed to restore corticostriatal LTD in P60 Tor1a+/Δgag mice (Figure 7D; p>0.05) confirming that BDNF-dependent alterations are limited to a sensitive period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: Pirenzepine failed to rescue the expression of LTD in Tor1a+/Δgag mice from p28 to p35.
source: Pirenzepine failed to rescue the expression of LTD in Tor1a+/Δgag mice from p28 to p35 (Figure 7E; p>0.05), indicating that distinct mechanisms underlie plasticity alterations at different developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E with statistical significance p>0.05.

claim: Distinct mechanisms underlie plasticity alterations at different developmental stages in DYT1 dystonia.
source: Pirenzepine failed to rescue the expression of LTD in Tor1a+/Δgag mice from p28 to p35 (Figure 7E; p>0.05), indicating that distinct mechanisms underlie plasticity alterations at different developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential responses to pirenzepine at different ages.

claim: The critical period for the onset of symptoms in DYT1 dystonia patients matches an early time-window of activity-dependent plastic changes in the striatum.
source: The critical period for the onset of symptoms in DYT1 dystonia patients matches an early time-window of activity-dependent plastic changes in the striatum, which shape motor memory and learning processes during childhood and early adolescence.
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of clinical observations with the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: There exists a critical period when SPNs exhibit premature LTP in DYT1 dystonia.
source: Our systematic analysis of functional and structural synaptic plasticity in DYT1 dystonia demonstrates: (i) The existence of a critical period when SPNs exhibit premature LTP
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing premature LTP in juvenile Tor1a+/Δgag mice.

claim: There is a significant increase of AMPAR levels in the postsynaptic compartment which correlates with the reduction of NMDA/AMPA ratio in juvenile Tor1a+/Δgag mice.
source: (ii) A significant increase of AMPAR levels in the postsynaptic compartment which correlates with the reduction of NMDA/AMPA ratio, the increased amplitudes of postsynaptic currents and the rightward shift in the AMPA I-V curve observed in juvenile Tor1a+/Δgag mice
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a BDNF time-dependent increase in expression profile which parallels the alterations in DYT1 dystonia.
source: (iii) A BDNF time-dependent increase in expression profile, which parallels the alterations described
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Abnormal plasticity is associated with profound changes of dendritic spine density and morphology in juvenile Tor1a+/Δgag.
source: (iv) abnormal plasticity is associated with profound changes of dendritic spine density and morphology in juvenile Tor1a+/Δgag
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A rescue of the synaptic plasticity deficits is obtained by in vivo administration of a TrkB inhibitor.
source: (v) A rescue of the synaptic plasticity deficits is obtained by in vivo administration of a TrkB inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Striatal LTP in mature tissue preparation or in the developing striatum is dependent on the activation of NMDAR.
source: Striatal LTP either in mature tissue preparation or in the developing striatum is dependent on the activation of NMDAR (Calabresi et al., 1992b; Partridge et al., 2000), whereas LTD depends on AMPAR (Calabresi et al., 1992a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Calabresi et al., 1992b; Partridge et al., 2000).

claim: Striatal LTD depends on AMPAR.
source: Striatal LTP either in mature tissue preparation or in the developing striatum is dependent on the activation of NMDAR (Calabresi et al., 1992b; Partridge et al., 2000), whereas LTD depends on AMPAR (Calabresi et al., 1992a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Calabresi et al., 1992a).

claim: Loss of homeostatic regulation of excitatory synapses in distinct neuronal subtypes involve postsynaptic changes in accumulation of AMPAR.
source: Specifically, loss of homeostatic regulation of excitatory synapses in distinct neuronal subtypes involve postsynaptic changes in accumulation of AMPAR (Lissin et al., 1998; O'Brien et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lissin et al., 1998; O'Brien et al., 1998).

claim: GluA1-Ser845 plays a key role in the synaptic delivery of GluA1-containing AMPARs by LTP.
source: Moreover, GluA1-Ser845 (Roche et al., 1996) plays a key role in the synaptic delivery of GluA1-containing AMPARs by LTP (Esteban et al., 2003; Bassani et al., 2013) and is involved in surface reinsertion/stabilization of AMPARs (Ehlers, 2000), thus providing a molecular mechanism for the observed increase of AMPARs at postsynaptic membranes in P26 Tor1a+/Δgag mice compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Roche et al., 1996; Esteban et al., 2003; Bassani et al., 2013; Ehlers, 2000).

claim: BDNF treatment acutely controls both AMPAR subunits and their scaffolding proteins trafficking, thereby modifying the strength of synaptic activity.
source: Indeed, BDNF treatment acutely controls both AMPAR subunits and their scaffolding proteins trafficking, thereby modifying the strength of synaptic activity (Minichiello et al., 1999; Mauceri et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Minichiello et al., 1999; Mauceri et al., 2004).

claim: BDNF plays a major role in spine maturation in several brain regions, including the striatum.
source: Yet, BDNF also plays a major role in spine maturation in several brain regions, including the striatum (Baquet et al., 2004; Rauskolb et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Baquet et al., 2004; Rauskolb et al., 2010).

claim: GluN2A expression increases from the second postnatal week to become widely expressed and abundant throughout the brain.
source: In particular, GluN2A expression increases from the second postnatal week to become widely expressed and abundant throughout the brain (Bellone and Nicoll, 2007; Gray et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bellone and Nicoll, 2007; Gray et al., 2011).

claim: There exists a close coordination between spine size and AMPAR levels at synaptic membranes.
source: Moreover, the existence of a close coordination between spine size and AMPAR levels at synaptic membranes has been previously reported (Kopec et al., 2007; Malinverno et al., 2010) and spine volume has been positively correlated with the strength of AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kopec et al., 2007; Malinverno et al., 2010).

claim: Spine volume has been positively correlated with the strength of AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
source: Moreover, the existence of a close coordination between spine size and AMPAR levels at synaptic membranes has been previously reported (Kopec et al., 2007; Malinverno et al., 2010) and spine volume has been positively correlated with the strength of AMPAR-mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kopec et al., 2007; Malinverno et al., 2010).

claim: The beneficial effects of Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) in dystonic patients is more effective in young patients, as compared to patients implanted later in life.
source: Our hypothesis is also consistent with the clinical observation that the beneficial effects of Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) in dystonic patients is more effective in young patients, as compared to patients implanted later in life (Isaias et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Isaias et al., 2008).

claim: Weeks are commonly required to obtain symptomatic relief following DBS in dystonia, and improvements may continue to be manifest over time.
source: Additionally, compared to the prompt efficacy observed in Parkinson's disease patients, weeks are commonly required to obtain symptomatic relief following DBS, and improvements may continue to be manifest over time (Vercueil et al., 2001; Krauss, 2002; Vidailhet and Pollak, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Vercueil et al., 2001; Krauss, 2002; Vidailhet and Pollak, 2005).

claim: The loss of LTD may be related to the aberrant composition of striatal AMPARs observed in mutant mice.
